original_question: For semigroup elements a and b, define a ∼p b to mean that there exist u and v in the semigroup with a = uv and b = vu. If a semigroup embeds into a group, must this relation ∼p be transitive on that semigroup?
target_in_paper: Section 1’s formulation of the open problem from [3] asking whether ∼p is transitive for every semigroup that can be embedded in a group, with the paper’s negative answer given in Section 5, Corollary 5.2.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right relation and the right scope. It uses the paper’s definition of ∼p via factorizations a = uv and b = vu with u, v in the same semigroup, and it asks exactly the group-embeddability/transitivity question highlighted in the introduction. It also stays narrowly focused on the paper’s intended problem, without drifting into neighboring questions about variants, other conjugacy notions, or the transitive closure ∼p∗.
missing_details: Make the ambient semigroup explicit: let S be an arbitrary semigroup, and let a, b, c, u, v range over S.
Spell out transitivity explicitly: for all a, b, c in S, if a ∼p b and b ∼p c, then a ∼p c.
Clarify 'embeds into a group' as: there exists an injective semigroup homomorphism from S into some group, i.e. S is group-embeddable.
State that no additional hypotheses are assumed: no identity element, finiteness, cancellativity, or commutativity assumptions are part of the problem.
If one wants maximal paper-faithfulness to the surrounding notation, note that the paper denotes the transitive closure of ∼p by ∼p∗, but that notation is not required in the question itself.
refined_question: Let S be an arbitrary semigroup, and define a relation ∼p on S by declaring that a ∼p b if and only if there exist u, v ∈ S such that a = uv and b = vu. If S is embeddable in a group, in the sense that S admits an injective semigroup homomorphism into some group, must ∼p be transitive on S; that is, must every group-embeddable semigroup satisfy: for all a, b, c ∈ S, if a ∼p b and b ∼p c, then a ∼p c?
justification: This is the exact problem identified in the paper’s introduction: after defining ∼p, the author states that Problem 6.4 from [3] asks whether ∼p is transitive for any semigroup that can be embedded in a group. Section 2 supplies the precise formal definition of ∼p and introduces ∼p∗ as its transitive closure. Section 5 then gives the paper’s counterexample, summarized in Corollary 5.2, so the refined question should remain narrowly centered on group-embeddable semigroups and the transitivity of ∼p itself.
